back: Leading through service to the team: understanding and meeting team members' needs and development so the team can perform at its best.

front: The servant leader's order of work
back: Purpose, then people, then process.
Promoting self-awareness; listening; serving the team; helping people grow; coaching not controlling; promoting safety, respect and trust; promoting the energy and intelligence of others.

front: Three main responsibilities of a servant leader
back: Facilitate; remove organizational impediments; pave the way for others' contributions.
A servant leader helps everyone do their best thinking and work, as an impartial bridge builder, instead of deciding and coordinating for them.
Anything that blocks or slows the team. The servant leader works to remove it.
The belief that people can learn new skills. Successful agile teams and leaders share it.

front: Project manager in an agile project
back: Moves from the center of coordination to supporting the team: coaching, fostering collaboration, aligning stakeholders, handling what is outside the team's reach.
Three to nine members.
A team that together has all the skills needed to deliver finished work without outside dependencies.
Team members decide who does what and how, and share ownership of the outcome.
Cross-functional team members, product owner, team facilitator.
The servant leader on an agile team: facilitates, coaches and removes impediments. Also called scrum master, team lead or coach.
A generalizing specialist: deep in one area, with supporting skills in others and good collaboration skills.
Deep in one area and rarely contributes outside it. Can become a bottleneck.
Flow efficiency: optimizing the throughput of the whole team. Resource efficiency: keeping each person busy. Agile aims for flow.
Teams lose 20% to 40% of productivity to task-switching. A person split across two projects is only 20% to 40% on each.
Several team members focus on one item until it is finished.
The whole team works on one item together.
Doing all the requirements, then all the design, then all the building inside an iteration. Wrong assumptions are found too late.
Colocated: everyone in one place. Distributed: cross-functional teams in different locations. Dispersed: each member in a different location.
Picking up useful information by overhearing teammates in a shared space.
Commons: a shared area for working together. Caves: quiet places for focused or private work.
A permanent video link between two locations so remote teammates can see and talk to each other all day.
A shared belief that the team is a safe place to speak up, ask questions, share ideas and admit mistakes without fear of embarrassment or retaliation.
Inclusion safety, learner safety, contributor safety, challenger safety.
Psychological safety was the most critical factor in team effectiveness. How a team interacts matters more than who is on it.
Admit their own mistakes and uncertainty, ask for help, set inclusive norms, make space for quieter voices, respond to challenge without defensiveness.
1 Problem to solve; 2 Disagreement; 3 Contest; 4 Crusade; 5 World war. The earlier the level, the easier to resolve.

front: Four questions an agile project charter answers
back: Why are we doing this (vision)? Who benefits and how? What does done mean for the project (release criteria)? How will we work together (flow of work)?
The team's social contract: team values, working agreements (ready, done, timebox, WIP limits), ground rules and group norms.
External: more experience, weak relationships in the organization. Internal: strong relationships, perhaps less breadth of experience.
